prompt_text: How to run a year-end fundraising campaign
response_text:
Run a strong year-end fundraising campaign by planning early, setting clear goals, segmenting your donors, and executing a focused, multi-channel outreach from late November through December with an excellent donation experience and prompt follow-up stewardship.[1][3]

Below is a practical, step‑by‑step playbook you can adapt to almost any nonprofit size.

---

## 1. Clarify goals and learn from last year

Before you write a single appeal:

- **Review last year’s data**  
  Look at: response rates by channel (email, mail, social, events), average gift, % new vs. returning donors, and which messages performed best.[1][3]  
- **Set specific goals**  
  Use **SMART** goals (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time‑bound).[3] Common year‑end goals:  
  - Total revenue target  
  - Number of new and reactivated donors  
  - % of donors giving on more than one channel  
  - Number of new monthly donors or upgrades[1][3]  

These goals will shape your calls to action, calendar, and donor segments.[1][3]

---

## 2. Build a compelling case for support

Your year-end message should answer three questions for donors:[1]

- **Why this cause?** What problem you solve and why it matters *right now*.
- **Why this organization?** What makes your approach effective, trustworthy, and unique.
- **Why now?** Tie urgency to calendar‑year impact, deadlines, or matches (e.g., “Give by Dec 31 to help 100 more families this winter”).[1][3]

Key elements:  
- Use **specific stories plus a few key stats**, not stats alone.[1][3]  
- Clearly quantify impact (e.g., “$25 provides a week of meals for one neighbor”).[3]  
- Keep your headline and main message simple and memorable.[3]

---

## 3. Segment your audience and tailor messages

Not all donors should get the same appeal.[1][3]

Consider segments such as:[1][3]  
- **Major donors** – Personal outreach from staff/board, 1:1 meetings, tailored proposals, specific impact, matching or challenge opportunities.[1]  
- **Mid‑level donors** – More personalized emails/letters, invitations to calls or small events.  
- **Monthly donors** – Thank and update first; then ask for a special additional year‑end gift or an upgrade.[1]  
- **Lapsed donors (LYBUNT/SYBUNT)** – Acknowledge past giving, show impact, and invite them to “come back” with a clear, low‑friction ask.[4]  
- **New and small donors** – Clear, emotional stories and simple, easy donation forms.[1][3]  

Use your data to decide **which channels** work for which segment (e.g., some older donors respond best to mail; younger to SMS/social).[3]

---

## 4. Map out a campaign calendar

Create a calendar covering roughly **Giving Tuesday through Dec 31**.[1][3]

Include:[1][3]  
- Exact send dates for email series  
- Direct mail drop dates  
- Social media pushes and ad flights  
- SMS reminders (if you use text)  
- Any events / peer‑to‑peer launches  
- Staff/board calling days  
- Internal deadlines (copy, design, approvals)

Be specific so the team knows **who gets what, when, and through which channel**.[3] Avoid over‑emailing the same segment by tracking overlaps.[3]

---

## 5. Use a multi‑channel strategy

Year-end is where **multichannel fundraising** works especially well: around 70% of donors give through multiple channels.[3]

Common mix:[1][2][3]  
- **Email series** – A structured sequence (e.g., launch, story/impact, reminder, deadline, last‑chance).  
- **Direct mail** – Letters or postcards, especially effective for older or high‑value donors.[1][3]  
- **Social media** – Posts, stories, live updates, countdowns, progress thermometers.[1][2]  
- **Website** – Homepage banners or takeovers that mirror your campaign theme and drive to your giving page.[1][2]  
- **SMS/text** – Short, deadline‑driven reminders, especially close to Dec 31.[3]  
- **Phone/1:1 outreach** – Staff and board calls for major donors and key prospects.[1]  
- **Peer‑to‑peer** – Supporters creating their own mini‑campaigns.[1][7]

The goal is **reinforcement**, not repetition: same campaign theme and case for support, adapted to each channel.

---

## 6. Craft effective year‑end appeals (especially email and mail)

Whether email or direct mail, strong year‑end appeals tend to have:

- **Clear, donor‑centric story** – Focus on a person or concrete situation, then link to the larger need.[1][3]  
- **Specific, manageable ask** – “Will you give $50 to…?” instead of “Please support us.”[3]  
- **Suggested giving levels tied to impact** – E.g., “$25 feeds 1 family, $75 feeds 3 families, $150 feeds 6 families.”[3]  
- **Strong, repeated call to action** – At least 2–3 times in longer pieces.  
- **Urgency** – Calendar year‑end, matching gift deadlines, or a time‑bound goal.[1][3]  

For email, tests show:[2][3]  
- Clear subject lines and preview text aligned with the campaign theme can significantly improve opens.[2]  
- Personalization (first name, past impact) increases response.[3]  
- Simple layouts with a prominent button (“Give Now”) outperform cluttered designs.[2]

---

## 7. Optimize your online donation experience

Your donation page can make or break year‑end results.

Best practices:[1][2][3][9]  
- **Dedicated year‑end giving page** that mirrors your campaign (branding, message, imagery).[2][9]  
- **Mobile‑friendly** design; test on phones and tablets.[1][3][9]  
- **Minimal required fields** to reduce friction.[1]  
- **Suggested gift amounts** aligned with your typical gifts and tied to impact.[1][3][9]  
- **Recurring gift option** clearly visible (e.g., checkbox for “Make this monthly”).[1][9]  
- **Multiple payment options** (credit card, ACH, digital wallets).[1][9]  
- Ensure your form is integrated with your CRM so new donors and gifts sync automatically.[3]

Test your form end‑to‑end—including confirmation email—before launch.[3]

---

## 8. Engage your board and internal team

Year‑end works better when everyone is aligned.[1]

- Provide board/staff with:  
  - A **1–2 page campaign overview** (goals, key messages, timeline).[1]  
  - Simple **talking points** and customizable **email/call scripts**.[1]  
- Give them **specific tasks**:  
  - Sending personal notes to top donors  
  - Making a certain number of calls each week  
  - Sharing posts on their own social channels[1]  
- Use checklists or trackers so they see what’s done and what’s left, and regularly share progress updates and wins.[1]

---

## 9. Execute, monitor, and adjust in real time

During late November and December:[1][2][3]

- **Launch** around Giving Tuesday or another strategic date.[1][2]  
- Track weekly (or more often near Dec 31):  
  - Opens, clicks, and conversions by email  
  - Gifts, average gift, new vs. returning donors  
  - Channel performance (email vs. mail vs. social vs. SMS).[1][3]  
- Make small, data‑driven adjustments:  
  - Test subject lines, preview text, or send times.[1][2]  
  - Adjust suggested gift amounts if many donors choose the lowest.[1]  
  - Re‑target non‑openers with slightly modified messages or channels (e.g., text to email non‑responders).[4]

---

## 10. Steward donors and set up next year

Right after the campaign (early January):[1][3][5]

- **Send timely, heartfelt thank‑yous**  
  - Reference their specific impact (“Your gift helped…”)  
  - Share an early story or result from the funds raised.[1][3][7]  
- **Report back internally**  
  - What worked, what didn’t, and what you will change next year.[1][5]  
- **Prepare for retention**  
  - Identify new donors to invite into welcome/drip sequences.  
  - Flag strong year‑end donors as prospects for upgrades or recurring giving.  
  - Store your campaign assets, results, and notes so you’re not starting from scratch again next year.[1][5]

---

## If you share a bit more…

If you tell me:
- Your type of organization,
- Rough email list size / donor base, and
- Whether you already use mail, events, or SMS,

I can draft a **sample 4–6 week year-end calendar** plus **one or two tailored email templates** you can plug in immediately.
